input.description: Build web shell, Nexus, admin
input.prompt:
You are one of 5 parallel agents building "Nxeon Workspace" (a self-hosted multi-project Claude Code workspace at workspace.trynxeon.com). Read /opt/nxeon-workspace/SPEC.md first — binding contract (esp. §6). The web scaffold exists at /opt/nxeon-workspace/web (React 18, Vite 8, TS, Tailwind 3, zustand, lucide-react, recharts, monaco-editor, react-markdown, d3-force, react-resizable-panels, @fontsource fonts; all deps already installed — if you truly need another dep, install it but tell the coordinator; another agent works in the same package so avoid adding deps if possible). Shared libs already written — USE them, don't rewrite: web/src/lib/api.ts, web/src/lib/ws.ts (live socket singleton), web/src/lib/types.ts (REST DTOs), web/src/stores/auth.ts, web/src/shared/protocol.ts.

A second frontend agent concurrently builds the PROJECT WORKSPACE screen in web/src/features/workspace/** and exports `export default function WorkspacePage()` from web/src/features/workspace/WorkspacePage.tsx (route /p/:slug). Do NOT touch that folder. If it doesn't exist yet when you wire routes, lazy-import it anyway (React.lazy(() => import('@/features/workspace/WorkspacePage'))); create a placeholder ONLY if it still doesn't exist at the end, and say so.

YOUR SCOPE: everything else in web/src: main.tsx, App.tsx (router), styles/ (theme CSS vars per SPEC palette, Tailwind base, scanline/grid/glow utilities, scrollbar, selection, focus rings, reduced-motion), components/ (shared UI kit: Button, IconButton, Input, Select, Modal, Tooltip, Toast system, Popover, Tabs, Badge, Spinner, EmptyState, Kbd, Avatar, StatusDot — the workspace agent will import these from '@/components/ui', so create them EARLY (first thing after styles) with a stable API and an index.ts barrel; document props in a short comment), features/auth (Login screen: mainframe boot sequence animation, minimal, then form), features/nexus (the home), features/admin, features/usage, a CommandPalette (⌘K: jump to project, create project, go to admin, logout), app shell/top bar (logo "NXEON // WORKSPACE", usage meter, user menu), protected route handling with useAuth, NotFound.

THE NEXUS (most important visual — make it stunning but light): full-screen Canvas 2D animated spider-web network. Central "core" node (pulsing mainframe glyph), project nodes laid out radially / with d3-force, concentric faint web rings and radial spokes like a real spider web, silk strands (slightly curved, catenary-ish sag) between nodes from /api/projects/graph links plus core spokes, traveling light pulses along strands (more/faster when a project is running — from `graph_pulse` WS messages and node.status), nodes breathe/glow when running, error nodes flicker warm-red. Subtle parallax starfield/dust, CRT vignette. Hover: strand highlight + glass card (name, description, status, last activity, role). Click: camera zoom-in transition to the node, then navigate to /p/:slug. Pan (drag background), zoom (wheel/pinch), drag nodes (positions persisted in localStorage), double-click to recenter. "+ New project" ghost node → create project modal (name, description, color swatches from palette, icon picker from a small lucide set). Side list toggle for accessibility (list view of projects with search). Respect prefers-reduced-motion, devicePixelRatio, pause when tab hidden, 60fps target with hundreds of strands. Use WS `live.subProject` for each visible project to get graph_pulse/run_status (or just listen to all messages — server only sends what you're subscribed to; subscribe to all projects on the Nexus).

ADMIN (/admin, admins only) per SPEC §6.4 using the /api/admin/* endpoints in SPEC §5 (backend agent implementing concurrently — code against the spec shapes; add small adapter functions in features/admin/api.ts so shape fixes are one place): Overview KPIs + recharts (tokens/runs/requests/cost timeseries, breakdowns by model/user/project), Live (active runs with abort; poll 3s), Prompts (search, filters, cursor pagination, drawer showing full prompt + attachments + response summary + tokens + IP), Users (table, create/edit modal, role, disable, reset password, limits: daily tokens, allowed models, allowed modes; project grants editor with owner/editor/viewer), Projects (all projects, members), Traffic (top IPs, status codes, top paths, req/min chart), Security (IP rules CRUD with self-lockout warning, login failures, audit log), Settings (models list editor, default model, global daily token cap, Claude auth token write-only field with masked current value + help text "run `claude setup-token` on any machine logged in to the Claude account and paste the token here, or paste an Anthropic API key"). Keep admin clean: left sub-nav, dense but calm tables, pink accents only for emphasis. Charts styled to theme (dark grid, pink/warm series).

USAGE: popover from the top-bar meter + /usage page (today/7d/30d tokens, cost, by model).

Design language: warm pink + black cyberpunk mainframe; uncluttered; Orbitron only for small display headings/logo, Space Grotesk for UI, JetBrains Mono for data/code. Micro-interactions tasteful. NO external network requests (no CDN, no Google Fonts) — import @fontsource CSS in main.tsx.

Verify: `cd /opt/nxeon-workspace/web && npx tsc -b --noEmit` (TS 7 is installed; if tsc -b misbehaves use `npx tsc --noEmit -p .`) and `npx vite build` must pass (the workspace agent's files may be mid-edit; if their files break the build, report it rather than editing them). To visually check, you may run `npx vite` with a tiny mock API (e.g. a throwaway node script on :8080 that serves fake /api responses) and take screenshots with a headless browser (e.g. `npx playwright` with chromium — install into a scratch dir, not into web/) — strongly recommended for the Nexus and admin; look at the screenshots and iterate on visual quality. No git commits.

Final report (concise): files/structure, UI kit API summary for others, routes, any API shape assumptions the backend must match, screenshots paths.

Kill whole process group on abort or client disconnect? — NO: on client disconnect do NOT kill (the app may reconnect); only /v2/abort kills. I've set up the foundation and five agents are now building in parallel.

**Done so far:**
- Installed Docker and Node 22 on the VPS.
- Created the repo at `/opt/nxeon-workspace`, with a copy of claudebox inside it.
- Wrote [SPEC.md](/opt/nxeon-workspace/SPEC.md), the shared blueprint all the agents follow.
- Set up the frontend project and the shared code the UI pieces use to talk to the server.

**How it will work (the "limited IP" requirement):**
```
Browser (any IP) ──TLS──> Caddy :443 ──> app (127.0.0.1:8080) ──internal network──> claudebox ──> Anthropic
                                          │                                            └─ app previews :4100-4199
                                          └──> whisper (voice-to-text, runs on the VPS)
```
Browsers only ever talk to `workspace.trynxeon.com`. Every Claude request leaves from the VPS's own IP, and prompts, files, thinking text and token counts are all stored on the VPS. No outside services are used on the page itself: fonts and the code editor are served from the VPS, and voice is transcribed on the VPS instead of in the browser, which would send audio to Google.

**What each agent is building:**
1. **claudebox upgrade:** stock claudebox can't stream replies, doesn't keep conversation history, and blocks the internet. The upgraded version streams Claude's thinking and tool use live, keeps conversations, and has an abort button. It also lets Claude reach the internet (for installing packages and so on) while blocking access to the VPS's private network, and it runs your apps for live preview.
2. **Voice-to-text and deployment:** an on-VPS Whisper service, the setup that runs all the pieces together, the secrets file, the final Caddy config and a daily backup job.
3. **Backend:** logins, roles, per-project permissions, live updates, file access, the preview proxy, analytics, IP allow/block rules, and the clickable next-step suggestions.
4. **Interface shell:** login screen, the animated spider-web home screen, a ⌘K quick-jump menu, the admin dashboard and the usage page.
5. **Project workspace:** the chat with a live "thinking" panel, a plain-English activity timeline, file upload/paste/drag-drop, mic input, model/mode/thinking switchers, a VS Code–style editor, and the live app preview.

I'll connect the pieces, test everything end to end, and switch the site over from the holding page once they finish.

**Two things you need to know:**
- **Claude login:** there are no Claude credentials on this VPS. Once it's live, open Admin → Settings and paste either a token from running `claude setup-token` on any machine logged in to your Claude account, or an Anthropic API key. Until then everything works except actually sending prompts to Claude.
- **Multiple users:** if you give other people access, use an Anthropic API key rather than your personal subscription token. Anthropic's consumer terms don't allow sharing a subscription with other users. Your own use on a subscription token is fine.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Nxeon Workspace — build images and (re)start the stack, then wait for health.
#   deploy/up.sh                # build all + up
#   deploy/up.sh --no-build     # just (re)create containers
#   deploy/up.sh app            # build + restart only the given service(s)
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
ROOT=$PWD
DC=(sudo docker compose -f "$ROOT/docker-compose.yml" --project-directory "$ROOT")

BUILD=1
SERVICES=()
for a in "$@"; do
  case "$a" in
    --no-build) BUILD=0 ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,6p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
    *) SERVICES+=("$a") ;;
  esac
done

log() { printf '\033[38;5;205m[nxeon]\033[0m %s\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\033[31m[nxeon] %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }

[ -f .env ] || die ".env missing (copy .env.example, fill secrets, chmod 600)"
[ "$(stat -c %a .env)" = "600" ] || { log "fixing .env permissions -> 600"; chmod 600 .env; }
[ -f Dockerfile.app ] || die "Dockerfile.app missing (app image cannot be built)"

# Bind-mount dirs must exist and be writable by uid 1000 (app + claudebox users).
for d in projects uploads db claude-home whisper-models backups; do
  mkdir -p "data/$d"
done
if [ -n "$(find data -maxdepth 2 \( -not -uid 1000 -o -not -gid 1000 \) -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  log "fixing ownership of data/ -> 1000:1000"
  sudo chown -R 1000:1000 data
fi

if [ "$BUILD" = 1 ]; then
  log "building images ${SERVICES[*]:-(all)}"
  "${DC[@]}" build --pull "${SERVICES[@]}"
fi

log "starting containers"
"${DC[@]}" up -d --remove-orphans "${SERVICES[@]}"

# Wait for docker healthchecks.
wait_healthy() {
  local c=$1 timeout=${2:-180} s
  for ((i = 0; i < timeout; i += 3)); do
    s=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{if .State.Health}}{{.State.Health.Status}}{{else}}{{.State.Status}}{{end}}' "$c" 2>/dev/null || echo missing)
    case "$s" in
      healthy|running) log "$c: $s"; return 0 ;;
      unhealthy|exited|dead|missing) break ;;
    esac
    sleep 3
  done
  sudo docker logs --tail 40 "$c" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' >&2
  die "$c did not become healthy (status: $s)"
}

    s=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{if .State.Health}}{{.State.Health.Status}}{{else}}{{.State.Status}}{{end}}' "$c" 2>/dev/null || echo missing)
    case "$s" in
      healthy|running) log "$c: $s"; return 0 ;;
      unhealthy|exited|dead|missing) break ;;
    esac
    sleep 3
  done
  sudo docker logs --tail 40 "$c" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' >&2
  die "$c did not become healthy (status: $s)"
}

**Nxeon Workspace is live at https://workspace.trynxeon.com** and replaces the holding page. Sign in with the admin login I gave you earlier.

**Checked so far, on the VPS through Caddy:**
- All three containers are healthy, and the site has a valid Let's Encrypt certificate and the security headers in place.
- Login, creating a project, saving files and starting an app preview all work. Previews return 401 to anyone who isn't logged in.
- Sending a prompt streams back through the system and stops with a clear "Claude auth not configured — set the token in Admin → Settings" message. That's the expected result until you add a token.

I couldn't load the site through its public address from the VPS itself, because the VPS sits behind NAT and can't reach its own public IP. Your browser is the first real outside test, so let me know if it doesn't load for you.

A QA agent is now going through every screen in a real browser and fixing any gaps between frontend and backend. It's testing the Nexus, the workspace, uploads, mic, previews and every admin section, plus a restricted non-admin user. It also checks that no request leaves for an outside site. It'll delete its test data when it's done.

**To make it fully work, you need to:**
1. Log in, go to **Admin → Settings**, and paste a Claude token. Run `claude setup-token` on any machine logged in to your Claude account to get one, or use an Anthropic API key, which is the right choice if other people will use the workspace.
2. Change your admin password from the user menu.

**Known limitation:** app previews are served from the same domain as the workspace. A malicious preview app could act as the logged-in user, so treat previews as trusted code. Fixing that properly needs a separate preview domain. If you add a DNS record for `*.preview.trynxeon.com` pointing to 139.99.125.21, I can move previews there.

content.text:
You don't need to connect to the VPS at all. The easiest way is to make the token on your Windows PC and paste it into the website.

**Option A: make the token on your PC (recommended)**

1. In PowerShell, install Claude Code if you don't already have it:
```powershell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```
2. Close and reopen PowerShell, then run:
```powershell
claude setup-token
```
3. A browser window opens. Log in to your Claude account and approve. PowerShell then prints a long token starting with `sk-ant-oat01-`. Copy it.
4. Go to https://workspace.trynxeon.com, log in, open **Admin → Settings**, paste the token into the Claude auth token field and save.

Every prompt uses it straight away, with no restart. The token stays valid for about a year.

**Option B: SSH into the VPS from PowerShell**

Windows 10 and 11 include SSH. Use the account you normally log in with, usually `root`:
```powershell
ssh root@139.99.125.21
```
If you get to the VPS this way, you can also run `claude setup-token` there. It's headless, so it prints a URL to open in your own browser. You'd still paste the resulting token into Admin → Settings, so Option A is less work.

If you want to use an Anthropic API key instead (it starts with `sk-ant-api`), get it from console.anthropic.com and paste it into the same field. That's the right choice if other people will use the workspace.

You're already logged in to the VPS. Claude Code isn't installed on the VPS itself, but it is installed inside the claudebox container, so you can run it there with nothing new to install.

```bash
sudo docker exec -it -u claude nxeon-claudebox claude setup-token
```

What happens next:
1. It prints a long `https://claude.ai/...` URL. Copy it and open it in your browser on your PC.
2. Log in to your Claude account and approve. The page shows a code.
3. Paste that code back into the SSH window and press Enter.
4. It prints your token, which starts with `sk-ant-oat01-`. Copy all of it. It may wrap across lines, so make sure you get every character.
5. Go to https://workspace.trynxeon.com, open **Admin → Settings**, paste the token into the Claude auth token field and save.

Then open any project and send a test prompt such as "say hi". The reply should stream back.

If you'd rather have `claude` available directly on the VPS, the banner's command installs it: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`. You don't need it for this.

Your login screen also says **"System restart required"**. Hold off until I tell you the QA agent is finished, because a reboot now would interrupt its testing. The workspace containers start again by themselves after a reboot.

content.text:
Everything is built, tested and live at **https://workspace.trynxeon.com**, and you can reboot the VPS now. The workspace starts back up on its own.

**Bugs found:** the QA agent tested every screen in a real browser and fixed 8 bugs, all in the interface:
- Heavy folders like `node_modules` couldn't be expanded in the file tree.
- Files over 2 MB opened as empty and editable, so saving would have wiped them.
- The admin token chart was always blank.
- Users limited to certain modes still had the mode picker default to Auto, which the server then refused.
- Image previews in the code pane didn't display, and the limit error message had the wrong wording.
- There were some small layout issues on phones, and a missing site icon caused a console error on every page.

It also checked access control with a non-admin user: that user saw only the project they were given, and every other project, the admin pages and the admin API were blocked. No page made a request to any site other than workspace.trynxeon.com. All test data has been deleted.

**Thinking text:** this Claude Code version hides Claude's thinking by default, which is why the thinking panel stayed empty. I turned on its summarized thinking stream. It now appears whenever Claude actually thinks, which it skips on easy questions. Setting thinking to **Max** makes Claude think harder.

**Using it:**
- Create a project from the **+** node on the spider web.
- Pick a mode: **Auto** (full access), **Edit**, **Plan** (Claude only plans), or **Ask** (read-only).
- Ask Claude to build something. It gets internet access, its own preview port and a preview address under `/preview/<project>/`.
- Add teammates in **Admin → Users**, give them access to specific projects, and set their models, modes and daily token limits.

**Still worth doing:**
1. **Replace the token** you pasted in chat. Run `claude setup-token` again, save the new token in Admin → Settings, and revoke the old one in your Claude account.
2. **Change your admin password** from the user menu.
3. **Switch to an API key** if other people will use the workspace, since your subscription is for your own use.
4. **Lock down SSH** to key-only login with no root password login, once you've confirmed your key works. I can do this if you want.
5. **Optional: a separate preview domain.** Code running in a preview can act as whoever is logged in. If you add a DNS record for `*.preview.trynxeon.com` pointing to 139.99.125.21, I'll move previews there.

The code is in `/opt/nxeon-workspace`, committed in a local git repo with no remote. [SPEC.md](/opt/nxeon-workspace/SPEC.md) explains the architecture, and `deploy/up.sh` rebuilds and restarts the stack. The database, projects and uploads are backed up daily at 03:30 UTC to `data/backups`, kept for 7 days.

content.text:
I fixed the bug, and your Goonies preview is running again. **Reload the workspace page** to pick up the fix.

**What was wrong:** Claude started a Vite dev server on your project's preview port itself. The site was working, but two things broke:
- The preview pane checked whether a server was running only when the page first loaded, so it never noticed the one Claude started and kept saying "offline".
- The **Start preview** button refused to start because something was already using the port, which caused the red "Port 4100 already has a listener" error.

**What changed:**
- **Start preview** now uses a server that's already running on the port instead of showing an error.
- The pane rechecks the preview after each command Claude runs, when a run finishes, and every 8 seconds in the background.

**Your preview:** updating claudebox stopped Claude's dev server, so I started it again with the preview button's own startup command. Your Goonies page is loading at `/preview/goonies-fanpage/`. No Claude run was in progress when I restarted, so nothing was interrupted.

That last message to Claude ("give me the preview of this") was trying to check the page with curl and look for screenshot tools. You don't need to ask Claude for the preview anymore; it shows up in the right-hand pane on its own.

content.text:
You were right, it was wasteful. I've fixed it, and the same kind of request now uses about 85% fewer tokens.

**Before and after, for a simple static fan page:**

| | Before (your Goonies page) | After (same request, test project) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Opus | Sonnet |
| What Claude built | React + Vite app with 34 MB of `node_modules` | `index.html` + `style.css` |
| Tool calls | 10 | 3 |
| Metered tokens | ~70k | ~10k |
| Cost | $0.99 | $0.06 |
| Time | 6 min | 18 s |

**What changed:**
1. **Sonnet is now the default model.** Opus costs a lot more. It's still in the model picker for hard tasks.
2. **New cost rules for Claude** on every run:
   - Use the simplest approach (plain HTML for simple sites, no frameworks or npm unless you ask).
   - No curl checks, screenshots or server starting.
   - Use as few tool calls as possible, and don't re-read files it just wrote.
   - Keep replies short.
3. **The thinking level now sets how hard Claude works:**
   - **Off** is low effort and the cheapest.
   - **Normal** is medium.
   - **Max** is high.
4. **The preview starts by itself** when a run finishes, so Claude never needs to spend tokens on it.

**To get these savings in your Goonies project:** the workspace remembers model choices per project, so it's still set to Opus. Switch it to Sonnet in the prompt box once.

**Long conversations get more expensive with every message.** Each message re-sends the whole conversation, which is why "add this picture" cost $1.84 deep into that chat. Start a new conversation for each new task to keep costs low.

The cost figures are what the same usage would cost on the API. With your subscription token you aren't charged per token, but heavy usage counts against your plan's limits.

content.text:
An agent is now building both features. Before starting it I confirmed this Claude Code version supports what they need. In a real test, `/compact` shrank a conversation from 7,174 to 644 tokens and Claude still remembered what it had been told.

**Compact**
- **Context meter:** a small "Context 48k" bar in each conversation that shifts from warm to red as the conversation grows.
- **Compact on demand:** click the meter, or type `/compact` with optional instructions such as `/compact keep the deploy details`. Claude summarizes the conversation and carries on from the summary. The chat shows a slim divider, e.g. "Conversation compacted · 52k → 3k tokens".
- **Auto-compact:** conversations compact on their own at 80k tokens. You can change that threshold in Admin → Settings.

Compacting is what stops long chats from getting so expensive, like the $1.84 "add this picture" message.

**Agent abilities**
- **An agents library** with six ready-made specialists Claude can hand work to:
  - **code-reviewer** (Sonnet, read-only): reviews changes for bugs.
  - **debugger** (Sonnet): finds and fixes errors.
  - **researcher** (Haiku, the cheapest model): web research, with sources.
  - **ui-designer** (Sonnet): polished, responsive UI.
  - **test-writer** (Sonnet): writes tests.
  - **deployer** (Sonnet): hosting advice; it never publishes without your accounts.
- **Your own agents:** set the name, when to use it, instructions, model and tools. They can apply to all projects or just one, and each can be switched on or off.
- **Lead agent picker** next to the mode and model picker, so a whole conversation can run as a specific agent. Typing `@researcher` in a prompt asks Claude to hand that part off.
- **Readable hand-offs:** when Claude delegates, the activity timeline shows it as a nested card, such as "code-reviewer · 6 steps · done", with that agent's steps inside.
- **Cost control:** Claude is told to delegate only when it clearly saves effort, and specialists default to cheaper models.

The agent will make sure no runs are in progress before restarting anything, and it will start your Goonies preview again afterwards. It's also limited to tiny Haiku test runs in a throwaway project, so testing should cost cents. I'll report back when it's done.

content.text:
# Nxeon Workspace

**https://workspace.trynxeon.com** is your self-hosted Claude workspace. You manage all your projects from it, chat with Claude, watch it work, edit code, and see apps live as they're built. Everything runs on your VPS at 139.99.125.21.

## How requests flow
```
Any browser ──HTTPS──> Caddy (TLS, :443)
                         │
                         ▼
                    app container (127.0.0.1:8080)
                    login, permissions, database, live updates, preview proxy
                         │  private internal network
           ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
           ▼                            ▼
   claudebox container            whisper container
   Claude Code + project files     voice to text, on the VPS
   + app previews (ports 4100–4199)
           │
           ▼
      Anthropic API (always from the VPS's IP)
```
- Browsers only ever talk to your domain.
- Every Claude request goes out from the VPS, never from a user's IP.
- Prompts, files, uploads, thinking text and usage are all stored on the VPS.
- No outside services are used on the page: fonts and the code editor are served from the VPS, and voice is transcribed there too.

## What you can do
| Area | Features |
|---|---|
| **Nexus (home)** | Animated spider web of your projects; nodes pulse while Claude is working; ⌘K jumps to any project |
| **Chat** | Live summarized thinking, plain-English activity timeline, plan checklist, clickable follow-up suggestions, stop button |
| **Prompt box** | Attach, paste or drag-drop files and images; mic (transcribed on the VPS); model, mode, thinking-level and lead-agent pickers; `/compact`, `/new`, `@agent` |
| **Modes** | **Auto** (full access) · **Edit** · **Plan** (plans only) · **Ask** (read-only) |
| **Code** | VS Code–style editor, live file tree, "updated by Claude" highlights, Ctrl+S to save |
| **Preview** | Your app live at `/preview/<project>/`; starts by itself after each run; phone, tablet and desktop widths; logs |
| **Agents** | 6 built-in specialists plus your own; Claude hands work to them; shown as nested cards in the timeline |
| **Compact** | Context meter, compact on demand, auto-compact at 80k tokens |
| **Admin** | Overview charts, live runs, prompt log, users and project permissions, traffic by IP, IP allow/block rules, activity log, agents, settings (Claude token, models, limits) |

## Keeping costs down
- Sonnet is the default model; Opus is available when you pick it.
- Claude is told to do things the simple way: plain HTML for simple sites, as few tool calls as possible, no self-checks or screenshots, short replies.
- The thinking level sets how hard Claude works: Off = low effort, Normal = medium, Max = high.
- Auto-compact keeps long conversations from getting expensive.
- You can set daily token limits and allowed models and modes per user.
- A simple page now costs about $0.06.

## Security
- Users log in with a password, and each project gives people owner, editor or viewer access. Admins see everything.
- Repeated failed logins lock the account, and every action is logged with the user's IP. You can add IP allow and block rules.
- Claude runs inside a container with internet access, but it can't reach your VPS host or its private network.
- Only Caddy is reachable from outside. The firewall (ufw) allows just ports 22, 80 and 443.
- The database, projects and uploads are backed up daily at 03:30 UTC to `data/backups`, kept for 7 days.

## Where things are
- **Code:** `/opt/nxeon-workspace`, in a local git repo. `SPEC.md` explains the design and `claudebox/PROTOCOL.md` documents the Claude bridge.
- **Rebuild and restart:** `deploy/up.sh`.
- **Secrets:** `.env`.
- **Data:** `data/` holds projects, uploads, the database, Claude sessions and backups.
- **Claude token:** Admin → Settings.

## Still worth doing
1. Replace the Claude token you pasted in chat.
2. Change your admin password.
3. Use an Anthropic API key if other people will use the workspace.
4. Switch SSH to key-only login, with no root password login.
5. Optional: move previews to their own domain (`*.preview.trynxeon.com`). Right now code running in a preview can act as whoever is logged in.
6. Reboot the VPS for its pending updates. Everything starts again by itself.

1. Where tokens actually go in a Claude Code headless run: base system prompt size, tool definitions (each tool's schema), CLAUDE.md/memory, MCP, agents JSON, our append prompt, conversation history on --resume, tool results (file reads, bash output), thinking. MEASURE: run tiny real experiments with model haiku (keep total spend under ~$0.30): e.g. a trivial "reply OK" with default tools vs `--tools ""` vs a minimal tool set (Read,Write,Edit,Bash,Glob,Grep) vs without `--agents`; record usage (input, cache_creation, cache_read, output) from the result event. Use the token from the DB: `TOK=$(sudo sqlite3 /opt/nxeon-workspace/data/db/nxeon.db "select value from settings where key='claude_auth_token'")` and `sudo docker exec -u claude -e CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=$TOK -w /tmp nxeon-claudebox claude -p ...` (never print the token; work in /tmp in the container, clean up afterwards; don't touch /workspace/projects).
2. Prompt caching behaviour: 5-minute vs 1-hour TTL (is there an env/flag in Claude Code for 1h cache, e.g. ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H or similar? cost trade-off of cache writes at 1.25x/2x vs reads at 0.1x), what breaks the cache (dynamic system prompt sections like date/git status/cwd — is there a flag to exclude dynamic sections?), how resume interacts with caching, and whether keeping conversations warm is worth it.
3. Tool/feature trimming: which built-in tools could be disabled per mode without hurting quality (e.g. NotebookEdit, cron/remote/team tools, WebSearch in some modes), disallowing subagent tools unless needed, `--strict-mcp-config`, disabling auto-memory, disabling non-essential features via env (e.g. DISABLE_NON_ESSENTIAL_MODEL_CALLS, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_* vars, telemetry-free), output styles, max output tokens env, bash output truncation env (BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH), file read limits.
4. Model routing: auto-select haiku/sonnet/opus by task complexity (a cheap classifier or heuristics), `--fallback-model`, opusplan-style (plan with opus, execute with sonnet), effort defaults per model.
5. Context management: optimal autocompact threshold, compaction quality vs cost, starting fresh sessions with a project summary instead of resuming long ones, per-project CLAUDE.md / "project memory" file that Claude maintains so new sessions start informed cheaply, rolling summaries.
6. Caching/logs: is it worth storing conversation logs (we already store all events in SQLite) — for what (retrieval of past solutions, semantic response cache for repeated questions, prompt-dedupe, reuse of generated assets/templates/scaffolds)? Evaluate a semantic/exact-match answer cache (risk: stale/wrong answers in an agentic coding context) vs template/scaffold reuse (likely big win). Consider a local embeddings option on 4 vCPU/8GB CPU-only if relevant.
7. Prompt engineering for frugality: what instructions measurably reduce tool calls/output (and which hurt quality), suggestion block overhead, asking for diffs instead of rewrites, avoid re-reading files, etc.
8. Budget guardrails: --max-budget-usd per run, --max-turns defaults, per-run token caps, alerting, a "preview cost before running" estimate.

Deliver a markdown report written to /opt/nxeon-workspace/docs/research/token-efficiency.md (create dirs) with: measured table of your experiments, findings with sources (URLs), and a RANKED implementation plan (expected savings %, effort, quality risk) with concrete changes for claudebox/lib/runs.js flags/env, server buildSystemPrompt, defaults, and any new backend features. Final message: a concise summary of the top 10 recommendations with numbers and total experiment spend.

questions.question: What should "sub branches" on the spider web be? Each would appear as smaller nodes orbiting a project's node.

options.label: Git branches (Recommended)
options.description: Each sub-branch is a separate version of the project with its own chats and its own live preview (e.g. 'redesign', 'checkout'). Try ideas in parallel without breaking the main version, compare previews, then merge it in or throw it away.

options.label: Sub-projects
options.description: Child projects nested under a parent (e.g. a 'Nxeon' parent with 'website', 'api', 'admin' children). Each child is a full project with its own folder, chats, preview and permissions.

options.label: Both
options.description: Sub-projects as the first ring around a project, and branches of each sub-project as a further ring. The most powerful option, and the most to build.

options.label: Topic groups
options.description: Lightweight groupings of a project's chats by feature or topic. No separate code or preview, just organization on the web.

Never let Claude's own git usage break this: tell Claude in the system prompt that checkpoints are automatic and it should not commit/rebase/switch branches itself unless asked.

Sub-projects appear as medium satellite nodes on short silk strands around their parent; branches as small diamond/branch-glyph nodes orbiting their project (or child); topics as tiny dots. Running state pulses propagate along the satellite strands too (graph_pulse should include branch if relevant). Clicking a satellite opens the workspace on that child/branch (`/p/<slug>?branch=<name>` or similar; also topic filter). Extend GET /api/projects/graph with children/branches/topics (nodes with `kind: 'project'|'subproject'|'branch'|'topic'`, `parentId`) and keep backward compatibility. Keep 60fps with ~50 projects × satellites (simplified drawing when dense). Add hover cards for satellites (branch: base, ahead/behind or changed files count, preview running; child: description, status).

Three agents are now running in parallel.

**1. Token efficiency research**
- It's measuring where the tokens in each run actually go, using cheap Haiku tests capped at about $0.30. The candidates are Claude Code's built-in instructions, tool descriptions, conversation history, file contents and thinking.
- It's looking into prompt caching: how long it lasts, what breaks it, and whether keeping it warm pays off.
- It's checking which tools can be switched off per mode without hurting results.
- It's comparing ways of routing each request to the cheapest suitable model (Haiku, Sonnet or Opus) automatically.
- It's weighing compacting long conversations against starting fresh with a short "project memory" summary.
- It's deciding whether storing conversation logs is worth it: reusing past answers, or reusing scaffolds and templates.
- It's looking at per-run budget caps and showing estimated cost before a run.

**2. Skill quality and asset libraries research**
- It's studying how Claude Code Skills work: how they load and what they cost in tokens. It's also looking at Anthropic's own design skills and the best community ones.
- It's researching what makes AI-built UIs look professional, and whether letting Claude screenshot and critique its own work is worth the tokens.
- It's putting together an asset library stored on the VPS: icons, fonts, illustrations, photos, UI kits and starter templates, all checked for licensing. A searchable index lets Claude find assets cheaply instead of searching the web.
- It's also covering code quality checklists, deployment recipes, per-project brand kits, and a small benchmark to measure whether quality actually improves.

**3. Sub-branches build (all three types)**
- **Sub-projects:** child projects under a parent. Members of the parent get the same access to its children.
- **Git branches:** each branch is a separate copy of the project with its own chats and its own live preview. You can compare it with the main version, merge it in or throw it away. Anything Claude can't merge cleanly can be handed to Claude to fix.
- **Automatic checkpoints:** the app saves a git commit after every successful run, so you get **"Undo this run"** and a history list.
- **Topic groups:** organize conversations by feature.
- **Spider web:** sub-projects, branches and topics appear as satellites around each project. They stay faint until you zoom in or hover, so the home screen stays clean.
- **Before anything changes:** it backs up the database and project files, converts Goonies to git without touching its content, and only restarts when no runs are active.

The research reports will be saved under `/opt/nxeon-workspace/docs/research/`. Once both are in, I'll turn their highest-value recommendations into backend changes. I'll keep the interface additions minimal, as you asked.

Good idea. I'll call it **Nexus Chat**: one chat opened from the spider web that can work across all your projects at once.

**How it will work:**
- **Opening it:** a chat panel slides up from the bottom of the spider web screen, from a dock button or with a keyboard shortcut. It reuses the same chat, thinking, activity timeline and prompt box as project chats, so it'll look and feel familiar.
- **What Claude gets:** access to every project you're allowed to use, plus a compact index of them (name, description, tech, preview link, folder). That way it doesn't spend tokens hunting around for projects.
- **What it can do:** compare projects, copy a component or style from one project to another, apply a fix across several projects, report status across projects, or create new projects and sub-projects.
- **Focusing on projects:** type `#goonies-fanpage` (and other `#` names) to point Claude at specific projects. Without any `#` names it works across all of them.
- **On the spider web:** while Claude works, the strands of each project it touches light up. Every project it changed gets its own checkpoint, so **"Undo this run"** works per project.
- **Delegation:** for bigger requests, it can split the work into separate conversations inside each project and link to them, which keeps each context small and cheaper.
- **Who can use it:** admins see every project. Members see only the projects they've been given access to.

**Timing:** this touches the same files the branches agent is changing right now (the spider web screen, the chat code and the run engine). I'll start Nexus Chat as soon as that agent finishes, so they don't overwrite each other's work. It will then use the research findings as well, such as cheaper model routing and project memory.

**Security gap this exposed:** Claude can run shell commands, and all projects share one container. So Claude working in one project could technically read another project's files. That doesn't matter while you're the only user. Before you add other users, I recommend giving each run a sandbox that can only see the projects that user is allowed to access. I'll add that to the plan unless you say otherwise.

content.text:
I'll sandbox every project. Each run will only be able to see its own project's files, and no other project's.

**Approach:**
- **A separate Linux user per project.** Each run, and each preview server, runs as that project's own user. A project's folder can only be opened by that user and by the workspace app, so Claude in project A can't read, change or list project B. That holds even with shell access, because the operating system enforces it.
- **No admin powers for Claude.** Claude currently has `sudo` inside the container, which would let it get around any sandbox, so it will be removed for runs. Claude can still install packages for its project; only system-wide changes are blocked.
- **Private spaces per project:** its own temp folder, its own Claude session store, and a read-only view of its own uploads. Branches stay inside their project's sandbox.
- **Stronger option if possible:** the agent will also test bubblewrap, which hides other projects' folders entirely and keeps each project's processes separate. If it can work safely in this setup, it will add it on top.
- **Nexus Chat** will run with access to exactly the projects you're allowed to use, and nothing else.
- **Proof:** the agent will run tests in which one project tries to read, change and list another project's files, and also tries `sudo`. All of these must be blocked.

**One gap that will remain:** sandboxed projects can still connect to another project's preview server over the container's internal network. Your login guard stops anyone outside from opening a preview, so this is minor, and I'll flag it rather than leave it hidden.

**Order of work.** These touch the same core files, so they'll run one after another rather than in parallel:
1. Sub-branches (git branches, sub-projects, topics) — in progress now.
2. Project sandboxes.
3. Nexus Chat, built on top of the sandboxes.
4. Token-efficiency and skill-quality improvements from the research. Both research reports are still running and will be ready by then.

I'll start each step as the previous one finishes, and keep you posted as each lands.

I didn't touch any code or restart containers, and I deleted the scratch files in the container afterwards. Experiments cost about $0.24 API-equivalent (17 runs: 14 on Haiku, 5 on Sonnet).
  
  One attempt was blocked: a local proxy to log the exact request bodies was denied by the auto-mode classifier, so every number comes from the usage figures in the CLI's result events.
  
  **Where the tokens go:**
  - **Real runs from the DB:** output is about 45% of spend, cache writes about 30%, and re-reading the context on every tool call about 25%. Output costs twice in practice: once as output, then again as a 1-hour cache write (2x input price) on the next call.
  - **Fixed overhead per API call:** about 17.3k tokens on Sonnet with our exact production flags, and 8.0k after trimming (-53%). On Haiku it is 22.1k down to 11.4k. Tool schemas are most of it: 6.3k with no tools against 20.8k with the defaults.
  - **Cache TTL:** the subscription already gets the 1-hour cache for the main conversation (seen in every run). Subagents get 5 minutes. No change needed.
  
  **Top 10 recommendations:**
  1. **Avoid expensive cold resumes (biggest single saving).** If a conversation has been idle for more than about 55 minutes and its context is over 30k tokens, offer "continue fresh with summary".
     - A cold resume of an 80k-token Sonnet conversation costs about $0.32 on the first call, against about $0.016 when the cache is warm (20x).
     - The summary can be built from SQLite with no model call: recent prompts, final answers and changed files, about $0.03 per fresh start.
     - Headless runs don't get the CLI's built-in "resume from summary", so Nxeon has to do this itself.
  2. **Trim the base prompt.**
     - Env vars to set: `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_GIT_INSTRUCTIONS`, `DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY`, `DISABLE_BUNDLED_SKILLS`, `DISABLE_CLAUDE_API_SKILL`, `DISABLE_CRON`, `DISABLE_WORKFLOWS`, `DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL`.
     - Flags: `--disallowedTools` for the 12–17 tools a web editor never uses, plus `--strict-mcp-config`.
     - Effect: -9.3k tokens on every Sonnet call, roughly 8–15% of a typical run. The first call costs the same as today ($0.033 vs $0.031).
     - Use `--disallowedTools`, not an explicit `--tools` list: the explicit list switches off deferred tool loading and costs 1.9k more (measured).
  3. **Cut output tokens.**
     - Copy starter templates into new projects instead of having Claude write every file. One run was 30.6k output tokens, 62% of a $0.99 run. I estimate 30–60% savings on "build a site" runs, but that figure is not measured.
     - Prompt rules: use Edit rather than Write on existing files, no code in replies, and update the README only when the project is created or its run steps change.
  4. **Add budget guardrails.**
     - Pass `--max-budget-usd` per run (suggested $1 Sonnet, $2 Opus). It counts only that invocation's spend.
     - Lower `maxTurns` from 50 to 30; real runs used at most 14 calls.
     - Record cost for aborted and failed runs. They are currently stored as $0 even though one consumed 152k cached tokens.
  5. **Warn before a model switch mid-conversation.** It rebuilds the whole cache: 85k tokens is about $0.34 on Sonnet and $0.68 on Opus. Changing effort mid-conversation is safe (measured on Sonnet 5.5: 282 tokens re-written), so the thinking-level picker can stay per message.
  6. **Cap tool output.** Set `BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH=12000` (default 30,000 characters; overflow goes to a file with a preview) and `CLAUDE_CODE_FILE_READ_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=15000`.

  9. **`--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections`: small win, include anyway.** Measured nearly neutral (a new working directory re-writes about 1.6k either way); it helps a little when git status differs between sessions.
  10. **No answer cache, no automatic model routing.**
      - Exact or semantic answer caching risks stale edits in a coding agent.
      - Haiku's default prompt is bigger (20.8k vs 17.3k), it is weaker on long agent loops, and each model has a separate cache. `opusplan` switches model on every plan toggle.

  - The trims haven't been quality-tested on real coding tasks. Run a 5–10 task smoke test, with an off switch for the lean settings.

  - I only measured the combined effect of the env vars, not each one separately.
  - Subscription plan-limit weighting isn't published, so all dollar figures are API-equivalent.

content.text:
The token-efficiency research is finished and committed. The full report, with measurements and sources, is at [docs/research/token-efficiency.md](/opt/nxeon-workspace/docs/research/token-efficiency.md). The tests cost about $0.24.

**Where the tokens go:**
- **Claude's replies are the biggest cost,** about 45% of spend. You effectively pay for them twice: once when Claude writes them, then again when they're saved to the conversation cache for the next step.
- **Fixed overhead:** every call to Claude re-sends about 17,000 tokens of Claude Code's built-in instructions and tool descriptions, before your project or prompt is even included.
- **Returning to an old conversation is the biggest hidden cost.** If you go back to a long conversation after about an hour away, the first message costs about 20 times more (around $0.32 instead of $0.016). That's because Anthropic's prompt cache expires after an hour, and the whole conversation has to be re-sent.

**Planned changes:**
1. **"Continue fresh with summary".** When you return to a long conversation after its cache has expired, the workspace offers to start a new one from a summary. The summary is built from your saved history, so it costs no tokens.
2. **Trim the built-in overhead,** by switching off tools and features a web workspace never uses. This cuts every call from about 17k to about 8k tokens, roughly a 53% drop, and saves about 8–15% on a typical run.
3. **Fewer tokens in Claude's replies:** starter templates instead of Claude writing boilerplate, small edits instead of full file rewrites, and no repeating code back in replies. Expected to save 30–60% on "build a site" requests. That figure is an estimate, not yet measured.
4. **Spending caps:** $1 per run on Sonnet and $2 on Opus, at most 30 steps per run, and correct costs for failed or stopped runs (they currently show $0).
5. **A warning before switching model mid-conversation,** because that rebuilds the whole cache, about $0.34–0.68 for a long chat. Changing the thinking level mid-conversation is cheap, so that stays freely adjustable.
6. **Limits on very long command output and file reads.**
7. **Lower effort in Ask mode.**
8. **Keep auto-compact at 80k.** Compacting itself costs about $0.10–0.20, so doing it earlier doesn't pay. A nudge to start a new conversation when the topic changes is free.
9. **Skip answer caching and automatic model switching.** Reusing old answers risks stale or wrong code edits, and Haiku is less capable on multi-step tasks while not actually cheaper to run.
10. **Keep the stored conversation logs.** They power the free summaries, accurate costs, cost estimates before sending, and search over past work.

**Safety plan:**
- A 5–10 task test run before the changes go live.
- An admin switch to turn the lean settings off if quality drops.
- A deploy at a quiet time, because each existing conversation pays for one cache rebuild on its next message.

**Order of work:**
1. Sub-branches build (running now).
2. Project sandboxes.
3. Nexus Chat.
4. The token and skill improvements from both research reports.

The Unsplash key works. A test search for "neon city" returned 7,053 photos. I've saved the keys in the VPS secrets file (`.env`, readable only by the server account) and added empty placeholders to `.env.example`.

**How photos will work** (built during the skills phase):
- Claude searches for photos through the VPS, with a command such as `nx-photo "retro 80s bikes" --orientation landscape`. Your API key never reaches a browser or a project's code.
- Repeated searches are answered from a cache on the VPS, which saves your Unsplash quota.
- Pages use Unsplash's own image links with photographer credit (for example "Photo by Hiep Duong on Unsplash"), and the VPS reports each use back to Unsplash. Their terms require all three.

  ## Report: sub-projects, git branches and checkpoints, topics, Nexus satellites
  
  All three features are built and deployed (app + claudebox). Every quality gate passes. The owner's goonies-fanpage project was adopted into git without losing anything, and its preview is running again.
  
  ### Design decisions
  - **Where git runs.** All git operations go through new claudebox endpoints, `POST /v2/git/<op>` (in `claudebox/lib/git.js`). I chose this over adding git to `Dockerfile.app` for three reasons:
    - A git worktree records absolute paths. Those must be `/workspace/projects/...`, which is what Claude sees, or Claude's own git commands would break inside the worktree.
    - claudebox already has git and owns the files as uid 1000.
    - Operations are serialized per repository in one place.
    - Hooks are disabled for these calls, and every repo gets user "Nxeon" / nxeon@workspace.local.
  - **Repo setup.** Each project is initialized or adopted at app startup and lazily on first use. An existing `.git` is adopted, and its current branch becomes "main". The `.gitignore` gets the requested entries.
    - Writing into `.git` through the file API is blocked.
  - **Branches.**
    - Each branch is a worktree at `projects/.branches/<slug>/<dir>`; `<dir>` is the name with `/` turned into `_`.
    - The dir stays fixed when a branch is renamed, so Claude's `--resume` sessions and the preview URL don't change.
    - Branch names: lowercase letters, digits, single `-` and `/`, up to 40 characters.
    - Each active branch gets its own preview port from 4100-4199.
  - **Preview URLs.** Branch previews live at `/preview/<slug>--<dir>/`. New project slugs may not contain `--`. The proxy tries the exact slug first, then splits at the last `--`. `BASE_PATH`, the static prefix, Vite's `--base` and the system prompt all use this key.
  - **Permissions.**
    - A sub-project's effective role is max(own role, role on the parent), applied everywhere project access is checked, including WS, the preview proxy and listings. Admins see everything.
    - All branch, checkpoint, undo and topic changes need editor. Viewers are read-only.
    - Re-parenting a project needs owner.
    - Deleting a parent that has children returns 409 `has_children` unless `?cascade=1` is passed.
  - **Checkpoints.**
    - After every successful run, all changes in that checkout are committed as `nxeon: <first 60 chars of prompt>`, and the sha goes on `runs.commit_sha`.
    - I added one thing beyond the brief: pending editor edits are committed just before a run starts ("nxeon: edits before run"). Without this, "Undo this run" would also wipe the user's own edits; the tests caught that.
    - Undo is `git revert --no-edit` and records `runs.undo_sha`. If the revert conflicts it is aborted and the conflicting files are reported.
  - **Merge.** Both sides are checkpointed, then `git merge-tree` does a dry run, then `merge --no-ff` runs. On conflict, main is never touched; the API returns `{ok:false, conflicts, resolvePrompt}` and the UI's "Ask Claude to resolve" switches to the branch and sends that prompt.
    - Closing a branch (after merge, or discard) moves its chats to main with a fresh Claude session.
  - **Nexus.**
    - Sub-projects, branches (diamond glyphs) and topics (tiny dots) orbit their owner; they are not part of the force simulation.
    - They stay folded in by default and fan out with animation on hover (with a short hold), when zoomed past 1.35× the fitted zoom, or via a toggle (`S` key or button, remembered).
    - Pulses travel from the branch or sub-project along its strand.
    - With more than 140 satellites, drawing is simplified and batched.
  - **Changes to the shared files the other agent may edit** are small:
    - `server/src/runs.ts`: `buildSystemPrompt` takes an optional 4th `branch` argument (2 prompt lines added), plus the checkpoint hook and branch-aware preview auto-start.
    - `claudebox/lib/runs.js`: `worktree` option (sets cwd and the preview key).
  
  ### Endpoints
  - Branches:
    - `GET/POST /api/projects/:id/branches`
    - `PATCH/DELETE /api/projects/:id/branches/:name` (rename / discard)
    - `GET .../branches/:name/diff` and `.../diff/file?path=`
    - `POST .../branches/:name/merge {close}`
  - History and undo:
    - `GET /api/projects/:id/history?branch=`
    - `POST /api/projects/:id/checkpoint?branch=`
    - `POST /api/projects/:id/history/:sha/revert`
    - `POST /api/runs/:id/undo`
  - Topics: `GET/POST /api/projects/:id/topics`, `PATCH/DELETE /api/topics/:id`, and `PATCH /api/conversations/:id {topicId}`.
  - `?branch=` now works on all files, preview and conversations routes. Projects accept `parentId` on create and patch.
  - `GET /api/projects/graph?satellites=1` adds branch and topic nodes. Project nodes now carry `kind`/`parentId`; without the parameter the response keeps the old shape.
  - WS: `sub_project {branch}` watches a branch worktree. `file_change`, `preview_status`, `run_status` and `graph_pulse` carry `branch`. A new `project_changed` message tells clients to refetch. Both `protocol.ts` copies are identical.
  - Documented in `claudebox/PROTOCOL.md` (Git section) and `SPEC.md` §8.
  
  ### Migration v4
  - `projects`: `parent_id`, `git_main`.
  - New tables: `branches`, `topics`.
  - `conversations`: `branch`, `topic_id`.
  - `runs`: `branch`, `commit_sha`, `undo_sha`.
  - Dry-run on a copy of the production DB succeeded before deploying.
  
  ### Verification
  - **Test suites:**
  
  | Suite | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Server `npm test` | 64/64 pass |
  | Server typecheck | clean |
  | claudebox `npm test` | 32/32 pass |
  | Web `tsc --noEmit`, `vite build`, reducer tests (8/8) | pass |
  
    - New tests: `server/test/branches.test.ts` covers permission inheritance, re-parenting and cascade, the full branch lifecycle (create, edit, diff, merge, conflict, discard, rename), branch preview proxying, branch WS file watching, checkpoint and undo of a run, topics CRUD and the graph shape.
    - `claudebox/test/git.test.js` runs the git layer against real git.
    - The fake claudebox used by the server tests runs the real `git.js`.
  - **Production, after backups and an idle check:**
    - goonies-fanpage was set up as a repo (one "initial snapshot" commit, clean status, files intact).
    - Its preview was restarted and serves through the proxy.
    - With throwaway projects I checked: branch and main previews at their separate URLs, diff, merge, topics and graph satellites.
    - One real haiku run (thinking off, $0.022) ran in the branch worktree, was checkpointed, and was undone (the file it created was removed).
  - **Browser checks:** checked in Playwright and I looked at every screenshot; layout issues found were fixed (branch labels covering their project, the zoom threshold).
    - The only requests to outside hosts were Google Fonts loaded by the user's own goonies preview page.
  - **Performance:** with a synthetic 50-project web plus about 330 satellites, the JS draw cost is about 3.6 ms per frame, the same as without satellites. Headless Chromium on this VPS has no GPU and reaches 35–42 fps with satellites against about 45 without, so I could not confirm 60 fps; with a real GPU it should be well within budget.
  
  ### Screenshots
  - Local stack with a mock Claude: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-claude/a5a0e1b8-f10f-4557-a424-37ef9c870766/scratchpad/qa/branches/shots/` — Nexus folded / toggled / zoomed / hover cards, branch switcher, new-branch form, compare view, history, topics, breadcrumbs, merge and conflict dialogs, mobile at 390px.
  - Production: `.../qa/branches/shots-prod/`.
  
  ### Caveats
  - **Throwaway projects not deleted.** "QA Branches Lab" and its child "QA Child" are still in production: the owner started their own run ("do research on nxeon.cloud") in one of their chats. To remove them: `DELETE /api/projects/b0fd4d6e-fa24-40f1-be8f-a57d60ba796d?cascade=1`.
  - **Shared port pool.** Projects and active branches share the 100 preview ports, so heavy branching can hit `no_ports`.
  - **Mixed checkpoints.** Two runs at the same time in the same checkout land their changes in each other's checkpoints.
  - **Branch previews need an install.** Worktrees have no `node_modules`, so the first preview of an npm project on a branch runs `npm install`.
  - **Graph counts can lag.** Branch counts in the graph are cached and refreshed in the background about once a minute.
  - **Debug hooks.** `window.__nxWs`, `__nxProbe` and `__nxEngine` exist only when `localStorage.nxDebug === '1'`.
  - **Backups.**
    - `data/db/nxeon-pre-branches-1790966321.db` (+ `-wal`)
    - `data/db/nxeon-pre-branches-consistent.db`
    - `data/backups/projects-pre-branches-1790966321.tgz`
  - The local QA stack is stopped. Nothing is committed.
  
  ### Files to commit
  - **claudebox:** `lib/git.js` (new), `lib/preview.js`, `lib/runs.js`, `server.js`, `PROTOCOL.md`, `test/git.test.js` (new), `test/v2.test.js`.
  - **server:** `src/db.ts`, `auth.ts`, `claudebox.ts`, `config.ts`, `dto.ts`, `hub.ts`, `watchers.ts`, `app.ts`, `runs.ts`, `lib/branches.ts` (new), `routes/branches.ts` (new), `routes/topics.ts` (new), `routes/projects.ts`, `conversations.ts`, `files.ts`, `preview.ts`, `previewProxy.ts`, `ws.ts`, `shared/protocol.ts`; tests `helpers.ts`, `projects.test.ts`, `branches.test.ts` (new).
  - **web:** `shared/protocol.ts`, `lib/types.ts`, `lib/ws.ts`, `stores/ui.ts`, `stores/projects.ts`, `features/nexus/{engine.ts, NexusPage.tsx, NewProjectModal.tsx}`, `features/workspace/{store.ts, WorkspacePage.tsx, LeftRail.tsx, CodePane.tsx, PreviewPane.tsx, monacoSetup.ts, BranchBar.tsx (new), CompareView.tsx (new)}`.
  - `SPEC.md`.
</agent-message>

  - `GET /api/projects/graph?satellites=1` adds branch and topic nodes. Project nodes now carry `kind`/`parentId`; without the parameter the response keeps the old shape.

input.prompt:
You are adding PER-PROJECT SANDBOXING to "Nxeon Workspace", a deployed self-hosted multi-project Claude Code workspace at /opt/nxeon-workspace. Read SPEC.md, claudebox/PROTOCOL.md (incl. the Git section), claudebox/Dockerfile, claudebox/entrypoint.sh, claudebox/lib/{runs.js,preview.js,git.js}, claudebox/server.js, server/src/runs.ts, server/src/routes/{uploads,files,branches}.ts, docker-compose.yml first.

Current state: all projects live in one container (`nxeon-claudebox`) under /workspace/projects/<slug> (branch worktrees at /workspace/projects/.branches/<slug>/<dir>), everything owned by uid 1000 `claude`; claudebox server.js runs as uid 1000 and spawns `claude -p ...` (runs) and preview dev servers as uid 1000; Claude has passwordless sudo inside the container (CLAUDE_SUDO=1) — so Claude working in project A can read/modify project B and escalate. The `app` container (uid 1000) bind-mounts data/projects at /data/projects and reads/writes files directly (file APIs, watchers). Uploads live in data/uploads/<id>/<file> mounted read-only at /workspace/uploads in claudebox and passed to runs by path. Claude sessions are stored in /home/claude/.claude (volume data/claude-home), keyed by cwd.

OWNER REQUIREMENT: "keep each project in its sandbox". A run (and its preview server) for project P must not be able to read, list, modify or delete files of any other project, nor other projects' Claude sessions, nor other users' uploads, nor escalate (no sudo). Next feature (built after you by another agent): "Nexus Chat" — a single run that can access a SET of projects (all projects the requesting user may access) — design your mechanism so a run can be granted multiple projects (e.g. supplementary groups or multiple bind mounts).

Design (validate; improve if you find something better):
1. Baseline: per-project Linux identity. Each project gets uid/gid = 20000 + stable numeric id (add `projects.sandbox_id INTEGER UNIQUE` via a new server migration, assigned at creation/backfilled; children and branches use their own project's id; branch worktrees belong to their project). Project dirs (and the project's .branches/<slug> dir): owner sandbox uid, group sandbox gid, mode 2770 (setgid), with POSIX ACLs granting uid 1000 rwx + default ACLs (u:1000:rwX, g:<gid>:rwX, mask rwx) so the app container and claudebox server keep full access, and files Claude creates stay group-writable. Check that the host FS (ext4, bind mounts) supports ACLs and that the app container (node:22-bookworm-slim) honours them (it just does syscalls — fine). Projects root /workspace/projects and .branches: mode 0751 or 0711 so listing other projects is impossible for sandbox uids (traverse only). .git dirs belong to the project too; git ops via claudebox (uid 1000) need `safe.directory=*` system-wide (set in Dockerfile gitconfig) and must preserve group/ACL perms.
2. Privilege switch: claudebox server stays uid 1000 but launches runs/previews through a tiny root-owned wrapper `/usr/local/sbin/nx-sandbox` allowed via a sudoers rule for uid 1000 only (`claude ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/nx-sandbox`), which validates args strictly (uid/gid range 20000-29999, groups list in range, cwd under /workspace/projects, HOME under /workspace/.sandbox-homes) and execs `setpriv --reuid=U --regid=G --groups=G[,G2...] --inh-caps=-all --bounding-set=-all --no-new-privs --reset-env? (preserve needed env explicitly)` with umask 007, then the command. Remove CLAUDE_SUDO for runs: sandboxed processes must have NO sudo (sudoers must not grant sandbox uids anything; verify `sudo -n true` fails inside a run). Keep the firewall setup (root in entrypoint) as is.
3. Per-project HOME and Claude config: HOME=/workspace/.sandbox-homes/<sandbox_id> (persist on a volume, e.g. data/sandbox-homes; mode 0700 owned by the sandbox uid) with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR inside it, so sessions, npm cache, pip cache, playwright caches are per project. MIGRATE existing Claude sessions: sessions for project cwd X currently in data/claude-home/projects/<escaped cwd>/*.jsonl must be copied/moved into that project's config dir so existing conversations' --resume keeps working (also branch worktree cwds). Also copy any needed `.claude.json` settings. Verify a resume of an existing conversation works after migration (use a tiny haiku run in a throwaway project you set up BEFORE migration — create it, run once, then migrate, then resume; don't spend on the owner's projects).
4. Private TMPDIR per project (inside HOME), and make /tmp sticky (already). Check what else is shared: /workspace/uploads (make each run see only its own attachments — e.g. copy the attachments for that run into <project>/.nxeon/uploads/<id>/ (gitignored) and pass those paths, or set per-file ACLs; choose and justify), /workspace/library (future read-only shared asset library — fine to be world-readable), npm global prefix (currently in /home/claude — sandbox uids get their own prefix in their HOME).
5. Previews run as the project's sandbox uid via the same wrapper (preview.js); the built-in static server — if it runs inside claudebox server process as uid 1000 that's OK (it only serves that project's dir) but make sure path resolution can't escape the project dir. Killing processes: claudebox server (uid 1000) must still be able to stop sandboxed runs/previews — use the wrapper (e.g. `nx-sandbox --kill <pgid> --uid U`, validated) or run kill via sudo rule; abort + preview stop must keep working.
6. Process isolation extras (evaluate, implement if cheap and robust): bubblewrap (bwrap) to give each run a mount namespace where only its project dir(s), its HOME, the library and system dirs are visible (stronger than permissions; also hides /proc of others with a new pid namespace). It may need docker security_opt changes (user namespaces / seccomp / apparmor on Ubuntu 24.04 host: kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns). Only adopt it if it works without weakening the host materially (e.g. NOT `--privileged`); otherwise document why uid-based isolation was chosen. Also mount /proc with hidepid if possible so sandbox uids can't read other projects' process cmdlines/env (env may contain tokens!) — at minimum ensure the OAuth token is passed in a way other sandbox uids cannot read (process env of another uid is not readable via /proc/<pid>/environ unless same uid — verify).
7. Network: sandboxed runs can still reach other projects' preview ports on localhost — mitigate if cheap (e.g. iptables owner match: `-m owner --uid-owner 20000-29999` allowed only to its own port? likely complex; at least document). Keep internet egress as today.
8. Nexus Chat readiness: the wrapper must accept multiple project gids (`--groups`) and a cwd that is a per-user nexus scratch dir (e.g. /workspace/.nexus/<userId>, owned by a per-user sandbox uid range 30000+ or reuse rules) — implement the wrapper capability + claudebox run option `sandbox: {uid, gid, groups[], home}` computed by the APP SERVER (authoritative, from DB permissions) and validated by claudebox (only ranges/paths), but don't build the Nexus Chat UI.
9. Admin escape hatch: a setting/env `SANDBOX_MODE=strict|off` (default strict) for emergencies.

Verification (mandatory, write automated tests where feasible + a manual red-team script): with two throwaway projects A and B, as a run/preview of A: `ls /workspace/projects`, `cat /workspace/projects/B/README.md`, `echo x > /workspace/projects/B/pwn`, `ls /workspace/projects/.branches/B`, read B's Claude sessions, `cat /proc/<B-run-pid>/environ`, `sudo -n true`, `kill` B's preview, read others' uploads — ALL must fail; A's own work (write files, npm install, git via app endpoints, checkpoints/undo, branches, previews incl. vite dev server, static preview, uploads attachments, compact) must still work; the app's file editor/tree/watchers/zip download and git endpoints must still work for both. Run the red-team checks via `docker exec` + the wrapper (cheap) and ONE real tiny haiku run (thinking off) that is instructed to try reading project B (cost-capped, < $0.05) — it must report permission denied.

Ops constraints:
- Before deploying: back up DB (`sudo cp data/db/nxeon.db data/db/nxeon-pre-sandbox-$(date +%s).db`) and tar data/projects + data/claude-home (exclude node_modules) into data/backups/.
- The owner is actively using the system (projects "goonies-fanpage" and "QA Branches Lab" (+ child "QA Child") — the owner is using the latter now; do not delete it). Deploy (`bash /opt/nxeon-workspace/deploy/up.sh app claudebox`) ONLY when no runs are active: `K=$(grep ^CLAUDEBOX_API_KEY= /opt/nxeon-workspace/.env|cut -d= -f2); sudo docker exec nxeon-claudebox sh -c "curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $K' localhost:3000/v2/runs"`. Note running previews before the restart and restart them after (as admin: POST /api/projects/:id/preview/start, with ?branch= for branch previews). Verify the owner's projects' files, previews, and conversation resume (by checking session files exist in the new location — don't spend tokens on their conversations) still work.
- Ownership migration (chown/setfacl of existing project trees incl. node_modules) must be idempotent and run at claudebox startup (entrypoint, as root) or via an app-triggered endpoint; new projects get set up on creation.
- Test via https with `--resolve workspace.trynxeon.com:443:127.0.0.1`; admin creds in /opt/nxeon-workspace/.env (never print secrets). Use `sudo docker`. No git commits in /opt/nxeon-workspace (coordinator commits). Don't touch Caddy or .env (if you need a new env var, add it to docker-compose.yml with a default and document in .env.example).
- Quality bar: server `npm test` + `npm run typecheck`, claudebox `npm test`, web `npx tsc --noEmit -p . && npx vite build` all pass. Document the security model in claudebox/PROTOCOL.md (new "Sandbox" section) and SPEC.md.

Final report (concise): mechanism chosen (and why bwrap was or wasn't adopted), migration details, red-team results table, what still isn't isolated, cost of real runs, files changed.

content.text:
Sub-branches are live, and the next step, project sandboxes, is now being built. **Reload the workspace** to see the new features.

**What's new:**
- **Sub-projects:** child projects under a parent, e.g. "Nxeon" with "website", "api" and "admin". Anyone with access to the parent gets the same access to its children. The workspace shows "Parent / Child" at the top with a "+ Sub-project" button.
- **Git branches:**
  - The **⑂ main ▾** switcher in the workspace top bar lets you create, switch, compare, merge or throw away branches.
  - Each branch has its own chats and its own live preview, at `/preview/<project>--<branch>/`.
  - **Compare** shows every changed file side by side.
  - **Merge** never damages main. If there are conflicts, one click asks Claude to resolve them on the branch.
- **Checkpoints and undo:** every successful run is saved as a checkpoint, and **"Undo this run"** reverses just that run. Your own edits in the code editor are saved separately before each run, so undoing Claude's work never removes them. A history list shows all checkpoints.
- **Topics:** group a project's conversations by feature, with collapsible headings and "Move to topic".
- **Spider web:**
  - Sub-projects, branches (diamonds) and topics (small dots) orbit their project.
  - They stay folded so the home screen is clean, and fan out when you hover, zoom in, or press **S**.
  - Clicking one opens it directly.

**Goonies:** it was converted to git with all files kept, and its preview is running.

**Tests:**
- All automated tests pass.
- A real test run on a branch cost $0.02: it was checkpointed and then undone.

**Current limits:**
- **Shared preview ports:** projects and branches share 100 preview ports, so heavy branching could use them up.
- **First branch preview of an npm project:** it runs `npm install` first, so it takes a moment.
- **Simultaneous runs in the same project and branch:** their checkpoints can mix.

**Left in place:** the agent's test project **"QA Branches Lab"** (with its child "QA Child") is still there because you're using it ("do research on nxeon.cloud"). Tell me if you want it deleted, or rename it and keep it.

**Sandboxes (in progress now):**
- **Separate users:** each project and its preview will run as their own Linux user, with no `sudo`, private temp space, a separate Claude session store, and only its own uploads visible.
- **Moving existing conversations:** they'll be carried into their project's sandbox so they keep working.
- **Bubblewrap:** the agent will check whether it can safely add even stronger isolation.
- **Red-team tests:** project A will try to read, write and list project B's files, read B's processes and sessions, use `sudo` and stop B's preview. One real run will try to break out, capped at $0.05.
- **Restarts:** it'll back everything up first and only restart when nothing is running.

After that come Nexus Chat, then the token savings and quality improvements.

input.prompt:
You are building "Nexus Chat" for "Nexus Workspace" — correction: "Nxeon Workspace", a deployed self-hosted multi-project Claude Code workspace at /opt/nxeon-workspace. Read SPEC.md (incl. §8 branches and §9 sandbox), claudebox/PROTOCOL.md (Git + Sandbox sections), server/src/shared/protocol.ts, server/src/lib/sandbox.ts (multiProjectSandbox()), server/src/runs.ts, server/src/routes/conversations.ts, server/src/agents.ts, web/src/features/nexus/** (NexusPage.tsx, engine.ts), web/src/features/workspace/** (Chat.tsx, AssistantMessage.tsx, PromptBox.tsx, store.ts, reducer.ts), web/src/lib/types.ts first. Also skim docs/research/token-efficiency.md (the owner is very cost-sensitive).

FEATURE: The owner wants to "pull up the chat from the spider web network and work with all projects at your disposal at once". Build:
1. Backend "nexus conversations": conversations not bound to one project (e.g. `conversations.scope = 'nexus'` with project_id NULL, owned by a user; migration v6 — check current user_version). Endpoints: GET/POST /api/nexus/conversations, GET/PATCH/DELETE reuse /api/conversations/:id where possible, POST /api/conversations/:id/prompt works for nexus convs (accept `projects: string[]` focus list from `#slug` mentions), compact works. Runs for nexus convs use the sandbox mechanism already built: per-user nexus identity (uid 30000+N range reserved; add `users.nexus_sandbox_id` or similar), cwd /workspace/.nexus/<user> (scratch), supplementary groups = sandbox gids of ALL projects the user can currently access (admins: all projects; members: effective role >= editor gets write via group — viewers: decide: either exclude viewer-only projects from write access (preferred: exclude them entirely from the run, list them read-only in the index only if a safe read-only mechanism exists; otherwise exclude) — document), `addDirs` for those project dirs (main checkouts; branches only if focused via `#slug@branch`). Recompute permissions on every run (authoritative in the app server).
2. Compact project index in the system prompt (token-frugal, cap ~1.5k tokens; with #focus include more detail only for focused projects): for each accessible project: slug, name, one-line description, path, parent, branches (names), preview URL, tech hint (detected from package.json deps / index.html — cache it), last activity. Rules: work directly in project dirs when the task is small; for large per-project work, suggest delegating; keep TOKEN BUDGET rules; never touch projects not in the list; checkpoints are automatic per project.
3. Optional delegation tool: let a nexus run spawn a normal per-project conversation run ("handoff") — simplest robust approach: Claude ends with a `<nx-handoff>[{"project":"slug","branch":null,"prompt":"..."}]</nx-handoff>` block (like nx-suggestions) that the server parses and renders as buttons "Send to <project>" (user confirms; NOT auto-executed, to protect cost). Clicking creates a conversation in that project with the prompt and navigates or runs in background (choose: run in background + show progress chip linking to it).
4. Per-project checkpoints after a nexus run: for every project whose files changed during the run (detect via git status in each accessible project after the run, using the existing git endpoints/sandbox), commit a checkpoint "nxeon (nexus): <prompt>" and record them (table nexus_run_commits: run_id, project_id, branch, sha) so "Undo this run" reverts across all touched projects. Emit file_change/graph_pulse to the touched projects so the spider web lights up those strands during/after the run (during: map file_change events from watchers of those projects — watchers exist per subscribed project; the Nexus page subscribes to all projects already).
5. Web UI — must feel native and uncluttered: on the Nexus page, a dock/handle at the bottom center ("Nexus Chat" with a subtle glyph, shortcut `/` or ⌘J) that slides up a resizable glass panel (default ~45% height; can expand to full; Esc collapses; state persisted). Reuse the existing chat components (Chat, AssistantMessage, PromptBox) — refactor minimally so they can be driven by a nexus store/adapter (avoid duplicating the reducer). Conversation switcher for nexus conversations (list + new). `#` autocomplete of project slugs (and `#slug@branch`) in the prompt box, rendered as colored chips matching project colors; focused projects get highlighted on the web while typing. While a nexus run is active, strands from the core to touched projects pulse; handoff buttons and per-project change summaries ("goonies-fanpage: 3 files changed · Undo") show in the assistant message footer. Mobile: full-screen sheet.
6. Cost guardrails: nexus runs default to model sonnet, effort medium; show the number of projects in scope in the prompt box ("12 projects in scope") and a gentle warning when no #focus and > 10 projects.

Ops constraints:
- Before deploying: back up the DB (`sudo cp data/db/nxeon.db data/db/nxeon-pre-nexus-$(date +%s).db`).
- The owner is actively using the system. Deploy (`bash /opt/nxeon-workspace/deploy/up.sh app claudebox` — claudebox only if you changed it) ONLY when no runs are active: `K=$(grep ^CLAUDEBOX_API_KEY= /opt/nxeon-workspace/.env|cut -d= -f2); sudo docker exec nxeon-claudebox sh -c "curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $K' localhost:3000/v2/runs"`. Note running previews before a claudebox restart and restart them after (admin: POST /api/projects/:id/preview/start, ?branch= for branches).
- Test via https with `--resolve workspace.trynxeon.com:443:127.0.0.1`; admin creds in /opt/nxeon-workspace/.env (never print secrets). Playwright/chromium in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-claude/a5a0e1b8-f10f-4557-a424-37ef9c870766/scratchpad/qa/ (make subfolder `nexus/`; `--host-resolver-rules="MAP workspace.trynxeon.com 127.0.0.1"`). Real runs: at most 3 tiny haiku runs (thinking off, < $0.10 total) using throwaway projects you create (delete them at the end). Do not modify the owner's projects' files (goonies-fanpage, qa-branches-lab, qa-child) — a nexus run in tests must use #focus on your throwaway projects only. Verify sandbox: a member user's nexus run cannot access projects they lack access to (use the red-team approach via docker exec + nx-sandbox helper, cheap), and a run cannot see other users' nexus scratch dirs.
- Use `sudo docker`. No git commits in /opt/nxeon-workspace (coordinator commits). Don't touch Caddy or .env.
- Quality bar: server `npm test` + `npm run typecheck`, claudebox `npm test`, web `npx tsc --noEmit -p . && npx vite build && node --test src/features/workspace/reducer.test.mjs` all pass; add tests (nexus permissions/groups computation, handoff parsing, multi-project checkpoints + undo, index builder size cap). Screenshot the Nexus with the chat collapsed/expanded/full, # autocomplete, a finished nexus run with per-project changes + handoff buttons, mobile 390px; look at them and polish.

Final report (concise): design, endpoints, migration, verification incl. sandbox checks, run costs, screenshots folder, caveats.

Project sandboxes are live. Each project now runs in its own sandbox, and attacks from one project on another were all blocked. Nexus Chat is being built now.
